Nothing else for a while. You can feel her *listening*, the way you can feel sun on your back with your eyes shut. It's slow and thorough, the way someone might run their hands over a strange boat before they'd trust it with their weight. The attention moves past you to the wagon, and lingers there. It comes back to you. It settles on your hem, where the salt is sewn. Then it goes deeper.

When she speaks her voice is old and dry and in no hurry at all. It's a voice that has outlasted a great many people who were.

"So." A tap of the stick on the cobbles. "You're the one who sent fire up my street to count what burns."

You hear her weight shift.

"And there's *two* fires in that pot on your wagon, which is one more than anyone sensible carries." A pause. The next words come slower. "And there's something else on you, child. Under the fire. Under the salt." Her nose wrinkles, very slightly. "Like a match struck in a shut room."

She doesn't tell you to rise.

Inside is one low stone room. Steps lead down to a basin cut into the living rock, fed by a channel from the sea, so the water breathes in and out with the harbor. The rim is painted blue and crowded with shells, sea-glass, a child's wooden fish, a wedding ribbon. Nell leads Karinna to a stool beside the basin. The old woman sits and folds her hands and waits.

If it starts to feel fast, that's the brake: go back to the book default, where the first trigger pays Karma and the rest pay Tokens.*

<tool name="Write">
<parameter name="content"></head>
<body>
<main>
<h1>Session 4 - The Hospitaller's Keys</h1>
<p class="sub">Level One solo playtest, Averond - Caria Greenhaven, Initiate of the Monastery of Strife. GM: Lilita. Played 2026-09-29/30. Counted as two sessions for advancement (split at dawn at the Ford).</p>

<details open><summary>At a glance</summary>
<p>A night and a morning. Caria brings Jem home to Dasha Korrin on a dark road, is visited in a dream by his dead mother, and learns what walks the coast. It's a ghola, and it's Brother Aubric: the Hospitaller who taught her to read the tenets, murdered and raised and walked on a leash toward Saltwind. She burns the leash out of Hierarch Calder's hands, takes Aubric's True Name as a gift, and lays him to rest in the reeds of Tanner's Ford.</p>
<p>In the morning she washes in the river, puts on a Healer's orange, and rides into Saltwind in mourning. The town expected a Monastery spy with a fire-demon. The blind keeper of Susheil's well-house puts the girl's hands in the sea's water and finds something else.</p>
<p>Ends at the well-house at midday, with Thousand-Voices sent for.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 1 - The Road Home</summary>
<p>Korrin's wagon stops dead. She reads the answer in Caria's face before a word is said, nearly falls off the box, and touches the boy's cheek like testing bread. "Mes Korrin, you'll skin me." "After I feed you." She wraps Caria in her own oilskin coat and offers whatever the mountain charges.</p>
<blockquote>"No mountain. Just me, an honest pilgrim, and Kade, and Hollis... and the tenets I was taught, whatever the men in that building say."</blockquote>
<p>Kade asks only a bowl for the dog, and that nobody write his name in anything. Caria falls asleep in the wagon bed, curled round the boy.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 2 - Tessa's Kitchen</summary>
<p>A dream, and she knows it: a south-country doorstep, a woman shelling peas who has Jem's mouth. Unlike Gram, this one asks her <em>in</em>. Tessa, two winters dead, stayed because her boy was neither here nor gone. She thanks Caria and warns her. Something that was a man once stood at the edge of the Ford's firelight, hungry and sad, with a string on it "like a dog's lead," and it has smelled her boy. It isn't fey. It's dead, with something under the grave-smell "like a match struck in a shut room."</p>
<blockquote>"Silver for the demon. Salt for the dead."</blockquote>
<p>For the warning, Caria offers payment in kind and carries a message for Jem: the barley, dry feet, and all the verses.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 3 - Salt and Blood</summary>
<p>She wakes gasping for salt. Korrin empties her fish casks without a question. A finger-thin line goes round eleven wagons and a thick one round Jem's. A drop of blood from the silver pin wakes the outer ring like frost. Ash from Asher's fire and two drops more wake the inner ring like embers, so that anything dead touching it touches him. Asher's patrol comes back with a confident all-clear. He's wrong.</p>
<p>"Like calls to like." Caria finds it by the smell of her own brimstone, forty paces out in the reeds, and it feels her find it. Her guided flame shows the drovers a grey, stooped dead man. At his belt hangs a ring of brass keys, and one iron key with a scrap of orange ribbon that she watched him tie when she was twelve.</p>
<p>She calls Brother Aubric to his wits by name and title and love, and he answers: "...Cari. Don't look at me, little sister." He tells her that someone walks him to the sea, "to the woman who shamed him." The leash goes taut.</p>
<blockquote>"How <em>DARE</em> you?!"</blockquote>
<p>Silver, fury, a Token and her brimstone go down the line together, and it burns out end to end. At the far end are candlelight, a tattooed scalp, burned hands and a high voice screaming. Hierarch Voss Calder knows her taste now, and she knows his.</p>
<p>Aubric gives her his True Name. His price is the one he always asked: <em>feed whoever comes to your back door hungry.</em> She lays him to rest with it, and the taint burns out in her salt. "Fire taught you something worth knowing. Well done, little sister." Then she holds what's left of him in the mud and weeps until the dark takes her. Kade carries her back to the wagon and puts the keys in her pocket.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 4 - Morning at the Ford</summary>
<p>A river bath behind Korrin's sailcloth, with every drover facing the oxen. She washes away the grime and the grief and keeps the indignation. She works to let go of the pleasure she took in Calder's pain. She thanks Grolikarnigan for footing, Susheil for water, Rana for cold clarity, Carterion for the craft of a warm bath, and Rikitak for the little spark. Asher, thanked to his face, has nothing to say for once. She comes out in the Healer's orange.</p>
<p>Kade is taking Aubric to the Saltwind churchyard, not north. He offers to shade his report to the Almoner. She refuses: <em>the absolute truth.</em> He will write that the Sister laid the Hospitaller to rest with his own name and hers.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 5 - Saltwind</summary>
<p>Korrin won't be paid for eels. She takes Caria's four silver "toward the boy's keep" and gives her the tooth-marked nail she dropped on the road: "worst trade I ever made." The sea comes up over the last rise. Old Bellows's coal nearly went out overnight, and it sulks until Asher tells it the whole story. After that it only wants to hear about the fire that burns on nothing.</p>
<p>Caria and Jem make charcoal mourning bands out of torn linen. At the gate, old Harl Pennock knows her by the white lock and the fire-pot and sends Davey running. Fennick, who once copied "misadventure: ill-chosen mushrooms" into the House register, says he will be correcting an entry. He tells her the orange suits her.</p>
<p>Blind Karinna comes down alone to see the Monastery's spy. Caria lays sword and staff aside and prostrates herself on the cobbles. Karinna names the penance: both hands in Susheil's water. The water steams, then holds her.</p>
<blockquote>"You're no spy of that mountain. You're something it made and couldn't keep."</blockquote>
<p>Caria won't accept that penance is done while her Order's wrongs stand. "Then stay and do more. Round here we call that being neighbors." Nell runs to fetch Thousand-Voices.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>People met</summary>
<table>
<tr><th>Who</th><th>What Caria knows</th></tr>
<tr><td>Tessa</td><td>Jem's mother, a shade two winters dead. She warned Caria, and her message waits for Jem.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Brother Aubric</td><td>The late Hospitaller, murdered and raised as a ghola. Laid to rest by his True Name and sealed against recall.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Hierarch Voss Calder</td><td>The hand on the leash. Burned. He knows her now.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Brother Anselm Kade</td><td>Burying Aubric in Saltwind. He will tell the Almoner the truth.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Clerk Fennick</td><td>Wrote the lie about the mushrooms. Means to correct it.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Dasha Korrin</td><td>Jem's keeper now. Traded a nail for four silver.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Karinna</td><td>Blind keeper of Susheil's well-house. Read Caria in the water and called her neighbor.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Nell</td><td>Karinna's guide, about ten. Stares at the white lock.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Harl Pennock and Davey</td><td>The harbor watch. Suspicious, but not unfair.</td></tr>
</table>
</details>

<details><summary>Rulings and canon from this session</summary>
<ul>
<li>Dream lucidity: a visited dreamer rolls Conjuror (or Level) against the dream's hold. A success means she knows it's a dream and a visit, and keeps her senses and Maneuvers. "Lucid Dreaming" is a Maneuver candidate.</li>
<li>Luck Tokens can be spent on any roll: your spirit's, another PC's, even an enemy's. The GM may spend GM Tokens on a player's roll.</li>
<li>Hooks: the owner may split her rank across the scene. Anyone else tapping it rolls it as dice. "The character <em>is</em> the power play."</li>
<li>A Boost and a Ward are separate rolls. Wards are wagers, Persistent and Reactive, with Area Effect free. A caster's own Ward doesn't fight her own spells.</li>
<li>A ghola carries a trace of demon: salt for the dead, silver for the demon.</li>
<li>A True Name freely given works as a strong Boost on the night it's given. The giver names the price.</li>
<li>Karma supply: the GM can pay Tokens instead when Karma runs hot. A double-length session can allow two improvements, but only one attendance Karma.</li>
</ul>
<p>Full detail, including the New-GM notes, is in the gap log.</p>
</details>

<details open><summary>Caria's state</summary>
<ul>
<li><span class="k">Advanced (two improvements):</span> Level 4, so 4 Luck Tokens a session and Down past 4. Spellweaver 3, with the new rank's Maneuver in Artifice 1. A third free known spell is still to choose.</li>
<li><span class="k">Karma:</span> 1 carried, plus 1 banked toward Conjuror 3.</li>
<li><span class="k">Wearing:</span> the Healer's orange, a charcoal mourning band, Korrin's coat.</li>
<li><span class="k">Carrying:</span> the Hospitaller's keys, Korrin's bitten nail, Bellows's coal (sulking), and the honey for the shrine-keeper.</li>
<li><span class="k">Owed:</span> Tessa's message to Jem; Aubric's price, for as long as she lives; the coal to the sea; Rikitak's empty bowl.</li>
</ul>
</details>

<details open><summary>Next session opens</summary>
<p>Susheil's well-house, midday, with her hands still wet from the sea's water, as Thousand-Voices comes down the hill.</p>
</details>
</main>
</body>
</html>
</parameter>

*Lilita's eyes light up a shade bluer.*

**Tanglebones.** Oh, that's *hers*, darling. It comes out of the brambles at the Court, the roots under Jem's hay, and the wind off the Ford. It's on the sheet as a known spell, not yet bound. Until she sits down with a pen and works out the binding, it's a full-ritual casting at bare Level. I haven't touched the design. That's her homework, and yours. But since I'm allowed to argue, here are three things I'd want settled before she writes it down.

**1. Whose ghosts?** This is the one that matters. If the spell borrows the local dead to do the grasping, it sits uncomfortably close to what Calder did: using the dead without their leave. She has just wept over exactly that in the mud. Your own phrasing points somewhere cleaner, though: *the individual pasts that claw and drag at us.* If Tanglebones wakes the *target's own* past to hold them, their regrets and their dead and the things they walked away from, then she isn't commanding anyone's ghosts. She's only showing a man what already has hold of him. That keeps her hands clean, and it's much crueler to the deserving.

**2. It ties into Hooks.** We've just ruled that anyone exploiting a Hook rolls its rank as dice. Grasping Ghosts could be exactly that: a spell that lets her tap the *target's* Hook against them. Someone with a heavy past gets held harder. Someone with nothing haunting them slips free. It's the rule we just made, turned into a spell.

**3. What it does on the table.** It's probably shaped like a Hindrance, with the effect as the strength of the hold. Take that as a starting point, not a recommendation. It should bite harder where the dead lie thick, or where the target's past is heavy.

All three are in the ledger as suggestions, not canon. When she's ready to write it, bring me her notes and I'll poke holes in them.

No, dear. I checked the ledger. Every improvised cast so far has been **one roll**, doing both jobs:

- the S2 staff light (Persistent + Guidable)
- the S2 flame in Rikitak's bowl
- the S3 fire in the Court's hearth
- the S4 Guidable flame

Each time, the one roll was the cast against a Difficulty that already included the Traits. A tie or a failure meant the hold failed and the spell was lost, which is why you spent Tokens on two of them. The margin over that Difficulty became the effect.

shaping-effects.md reads as **two** steps. First a free-action roll to hold the altered spell together against the raised Difficulty. Then, if it holds, "it casts normally," which means a separate ordinary cast roll for the effect.

The two readings play differently:

- **One roll (what we've been doing):** faster, but the Trait Difficulty comes straight off her effect. The Guidable flame would have been effect 4 instead of 3, and the Court hearth effect 3 or better.
- **Two rolls (the page):** the risk of losing the spell sits entirely in the hold roll. The effect comes out clean, but there are two chances for the dice to go wrong. Though a failed *cast* roll only fizzles, unless it's an Extreme failure.

So the merged version has been quietly taxing her effect on every improvised spell. It's added to the gap log as UNCLEAR, because "casts normally" can be read either way. Which did you intend?

Done, and fair. "More effective by making it less effective" is exactly the trap the merged roll fell into. I made Traits a tax on her effect when they should be a risk on the working. From S5 on we'll use the book's two steps:

1. **Hold:** a free-action roll against the raised Difficulty. If it fails, the spell falls apart and nothing happens. It's destabilized and lost until she rebinds it.
2. **Cast:** if the hold succeeds, the spell rolls at full power, the way it would without the Traits.

Tokens and the Hook can go on either roll, as usual. The past casts stand as they were rolled. No retcons, since the fire in the Court's hearth hardly needs a bigger number.

I've logged your intent as settled. I've also suggested one line for shaping-effects.md: "then roll the cast normally." That's enough to close the ambiguity for the next reader.

I've also added the comparison as something for us to look at. I'll watch how the two-step plays from my side of the table: the extra beat, the pacing, whether the tension of the hold roll earns its time. Then we can write up both methods side by side once we have real play to compare.

<*Session 5. You're Level 4 now, so 4/4 Tokens. The attendance Karma brings you to 2 carried, plus the Conjuror earmark. The Hook is fresh, with 3 to spend.*>

The cold gets into your wet hands quickly. You stand in it anyway, with the harbor wind snatching at the orange, your palms lifted to the grey-green water and the tears running freely. You don't know when the weeping turned into laughing. It isn't pretty laughter. It's hiccuping and helpless, and it comes from the same deep place the tears came from, only facing the other way.

Up on the harbor street, doors that had been cracked open creak a little wider.

The woman comes down the last of the hill with Nell trotting at her side. She's barefoot on the cold cobbles, and she doesn't seem to feel it. She's perhaps ten years older than you, weathered brown by salt and wind, with a grey shawl knotted over a plain dark dress and hair so stiff with sea-spray it barely moves in the breeze. A waterskin hangs at her hip. As she nears, something inside it catches the light. A ripple runs along the leather that has nothing to do with her stride.

Her eyes are on you long before she reaches you, and they aren't quite her ordinary eyes. You know that look from the inside. The Third Eye is open. She's reading you the way you'd read a stranger's letter: the grief and the joy knotted together, the salt in your hem, the match struck in the dark of you. Past you, the clay pot on the well-house step, where two fires sit very still. And something fainter, a thin warm thread running off inland from somewhere under your breastbone.

She doesn't interrupt.

Mira sets the net aside when she sees what's in your hand. She stands, wipes her fingers on her skirt, and takes the letter in both hands, the way you'd take bread at an altar.

She turns it over. The seal is a small, careful salamander pressed into red wax. Her eyes go doubled, and you know she's seeing what you saw on the road: a tiny watching spark bedded in the wax, like an ember in ash.

The spark looks at her. Then it looks past her, at you. Then it gives the smallest satisfied flicker and goes out, like a cat closing its eyes on a warm step.

On the hearth-log, Asher sits up so straight he's practically a candle-flame. *That's the Precentor's,* he breathes. *One of his.* He sounds impressed despite himself.

Mira breaks the seal with her thumb and reads standing, with the window's last light over her shoulder. She reads it twice. Her face gives very little away. Once her mouth tightens. Once, near the end, it softens.

She folds it again along its creases and holds it for a moment against her chest.

"Your Precentor writes a fine, careful hand," she says. "He has a great deal to say about priests, and property, and who rides on caravans." Her eyes come up to yours. "And at the end he asks me to judge you for myself."

She tucks the letter into her bodice.

You keep a lever whole until you need to pull it."

She lets that sit, and doesn't say the rest: that a lever which breaks is no use to anyone, and that someone in the west wing may not have cared.

"Your Precentor offers me the shelter of his friends," she says after a while, tapping the folded letter beside her bowl. "I don't know who his friends are, or how far they reach. I'd guess you know more about that than I do." A short, dry breath through her nose. "Or you don't. Either way, I've known you half a day, and I'm already sure you'd tell me which."

Out in the dark the surf keeps breaking on the Teeth. On the hearth, Old Bellows has stopped sulking. He is only listening now.

Mira drinks her tea and waits, in no hurry at all.

At *Finder Kade* she tips her head, working something through. "The lean one with the grey dog? I saw him this morning, from the churchyard wall. He carried the bundle up the hill himself. The tea has cooled enough to drink. It tastes green and salty-sweet, like the cliffs smell.

Then the door knocks against its frame. It isn't a real knock, more the bump of someone trying to open it with an elbow because his arms are full.

Mira doesn't turn round. "It sticks. Lift it."

The latch rattles and the driftwood door scrapes open on the dark and the surf. A small figure stands on the threshold, no taller than Nell, with an armload of wet driftwood and a string of mussels hanging from one wrist. He's thin the way a stray dog is thin, all joints and ears, with grey-green skin gone blotchy with cold and a patched jacket that has plainly been cut down from somebody's coat.

He takes one step in, and stops.

His nose wrinkles. His ears go flat. His eyes are large and dark and very much awake, and they go past Mira, past Asher on the hearth-log, and fix on *you*. On the orange robe, and on something he can smell under it.

He doesn't drop the wood. He holds it tighter.

He limps in on the club foot. The step-and-drag is so practiced you'd barely notice it, except that he stops dead halfway through it. He has one ear, a ragged notch of cartilage where the other should be, and it lies flat to his skull. One eye is dark and very sharp. The other is milky as a pearl, and somehow it's looking at you too.

Mira still hasn't turned round. "Min," she says, the way you'd set a hand on a skittish dog's back. "She's a guest. Under my roof. Under the Accords."

The word does something to him. His shoulders drop half an inch, as if *Accords* were a wall he could stand behind. He sniffs, carefully, and it's plain he doesn't like what he smells.

"Guest," he says. His voice is a hoarse little rasp, and every word comes out weighed. "Guest is guest. Min know guest." The good eye narrows at your robe. "Guest smell like *Hobbe-fire*."

The mussels on his wrist drip on the doorsill. Nobody moves.

Then he sees the hearth.

Old Bellows sits settled into the edge of the peat. Asher, bright as a new penny, has his light pulled in tight as if he could pass for a coal. Two strange fires on *his* hearth. Min's jaw drops open on a row of small, sharp, uneven teeth.

"*You*," he says to Asher, with deep and personal outrage. "Sneaky-spark. You go past in the dark, many moons back, asking *what burn*. Min *feel* you." He lifts the driftwood like evidence. "Now you sit on Min's fire."

Asher gives off a small, strangled crackle. It's the sound of a sprite who has just remembered that someone *did* notice him, and that it was reported to exactly the wrong people.

Mira takes a slow sip of her tea. Her eyes are dancing, though the rest of her face keeps perfectly straight.

When your hand lands on her knee, Bett flinches, as you knew she would. She doesn't pull away. She sits rigid and listens, and you watch the words go into her one at a time, like nails into wet wood.

*Strife.* *Medicine.* *Fire.* At *fire is a teacher* her eyes go to the hearth, and to the old red coal glowing in its pot as if it's listening.

At *Aubric*, her face opens.

"*Brother Aubric?*" The cup tilts in her hand. "He set my Hal's hand. Winch took two fingers off it, eight years back. He sat up with him three nights..." She stops. "They said the mountain men carried a dead Brother up the hill this morning. I never thought..." Her mouth works. "*Him?*"

You don't answer. You don't need to. She reads it on your arm, in the charcoal.

"We still feed them," she says, very quietly. "At the back door. Hal says it's bad luck not to. He doesn't even remember why." Her eyes are wet. "We'll come. All of us."

Then comes the edge, and she takes it like a slap. Her chin comes up, her cheeks flush, her mouth opens to argue.

And closes again.

She looks past you at the pallet for a long moment, at the small chest rising and falling. When she looks back, the anger has gone somewhere else. What's left is harder and plainer: the face of a woman who has buried drowned men and knows that the sea's rules are written in them.

"Calm," she says. "Aye." She nods once, hard. "I'll hold it this time. I swear I will."

She sets the cup down. Her hands have stopped shaking.

"Last one from your mountain came through here," she says, low, "his man broke my Jory's collarbone on his own doorstep. With a cudgel. For not *moving*." She wipes her face with the heel of her hand and looks at you straight on, a long, measuring look, fisherwife to Sister.

"You're not that."

It isn't a question.

Behind you, Mira has sat down on the edge of the box-bed with her arms folded, and she's smiling at the floor.

It's the sound of a girl who has just said out loud the thing she was most afraid was true.

Your tears run through your fingers and drop into the tide-pool.

They don't spread. They don't mix. Each one lands and *holds*, a tiny bright bead sitting on the still surface. Then, one after another, they're drawn gently up into the shimmering woman as she bends over you.

*<Tears are water,>* Shimmer says, very softly. *<These are mine too.>*

Something cool touches your brow, light and wet, like the first drop of rain on a hot day. It's a hand, or near enough, laid across your forehead. It doesn't try to stop the crying. It only rests there, cold against the fever in you.

*<Water knows what fire wants, Sister.>* The voice is right at your ear, the sound of a spring deep underground. *<Fire always wants more. It's the nature of the thing. That is why it must be tended.>* A pause, and a ripple that could almost be a laugh, very gentle. *<You told it to water. That was wise. Water is the one thing it cannot burn.>*

Footsteps come quietly across the wet sand. Mira doesn't ask anything. She kneels down behind you and lays one warm, calloused hand flat between your shoulder blades, and leaves it there.

Out past the rocks, the sea goes on breathing out, slow and grey and endless.

In the pot beside your knee, Old Bellows has dimmed himself to a patient, respectful glow. He's an old forge-fire who has seen a great many apprentices weep over their first burn, and he's content to wait until you're ready.

Mira's hand stays on your back as you walk out together across the wet, rippled sand, following the sea as it draws back. Shimmer goes with you. You lower him in.

Through it, beside you, Mira throws her head back, and a voice comes out of her that isn't hers. It's deep and gravelly and rough as a bellows-board, and it roars with *joy*:

The steam thins. The water stills. Shimmer opens her hands.

In the bowl of the ladle lies Bellows's coal, changed. It's black now, and gleaming, hard and glassy as a bead of jet. But when you tip it toward the rising light, far down in its heart a single small ember is still glowing, steady and red. Tempered, not drowned.

Mira's voice comes again, still his, quieter now and almost gruff with feeling. "Good girl. *Good* girl." A harrumph. "Carry me home to my forge, when your road bends that way. I've a story now that no fire in Averond can match, and I want to see the boy's face when I tell it."

Then Mira blinks, sways, and is only herself again, laughing and wiping salt-spray out of her eyes.

Behind you, the sun comes up over the cliff and lays gold across the Gallows Teeth.

The path down from the cliff is bright and steep. Mirna's son's net drags at your shoulder like a wet dog that has decided to love you.

Saltwind by morning is a different place from Saltwind at midday. Wives in the doorways shake out blankets. Old men sit on upturned boats, mending pots. Children run between the drying-racks with gulls screaming over them. Eyes find you, the orange robe and the white lock. Some slide away. A few hold. One old man on a boat-keel lifts two fingers from his pipe, the barest nod, and goes back to his mending.

At the racks a broad woman with forearms like hams takes the net off you without being asked, shakes it out, and runs her thumb over the mended place. She frowns. "These aren't Mira's knots." She squints at you. "Whose?"

Then you're climbing the cobbled lane to the well-house, where the spring comes up under its little stone roof, and the bench beside the door is already occupied.

Karinna sits with her stick across her knees and her face turned up to the thin sun, eyes milky and unmoving. Nell is perched beside her, swinging her legs. Nell sees you first and opens her mouth.

Karinna gets there before her.

"Peat smoke," the old woman says, not turning her head. "Brine. Applewood." Her nostrils flare. "And a sick child's sweat." A long pause. "You've been *working*, Sister."

The weather has turned toward winter and her joints know it before the gulls do.

Then there's the thing that makes your breath catch. Those are the hands she reads people with. You remember her putting *yours* into the water yesterday. It's not curable. Master Aubric's voice comes back, dry and kind: *Some things you mend. Some things you keep company.* But it can be *kept company*, a good deal better than it is now.

In your satchel are willowbark, rosemary, and the little crock of oil. Up on the cliff, a fire-sprite is keeping a whole hearth warm for the pleasure of it.

You squint up past the well-house roof. The sun has climbed about a hand and a half above the eastern hills: low, pale, and in no hurry. Late-autumn light. The dew is still beaded on the gorse up the lane. The early office rang a while ago, while you were coming down the cliff.

That leaves you a good three hours before the noon bell. Call it two and a half, if you want to be back here before Mira and not running up the churchyard hill at the last moment with your skirts in your fists.

It's long enough for a few errands, if you don't dawdle at any of them. It's not long enough for all of them, and certainly not with a sleep and a bath in there too.

And your body has opinions of its own. You've had perhaps four hours of broken sleep on a pile of nets. Your ribs still ache from the breastplate, and there's a gritty feeling behind your eyes. You're running on purpose, honey-water, and half a mussel. None of that is going to last the day.

Saltwind sits laid out below the well-house like a map. The harbor wall and Harl Pennock's stores are down to the left. The long timber lodge is in the middle, smoke rising from its roof-hole. Further along, at the far end past the warehouse, is the black smudge of the try-pots. You'd know it even without looking: the wind is coming off it. The warehouse doors stand open, and Korrin's wagons are drawn up in a row, oxen out of the traces, drovers rolling barrels down planks.

Up the other way, on the hill over the village, the churchyard wall stands grey against the sky, with a single thin figure beside the gate and something low and grey lying at its feet.

It's steep and cobbled, and then just steep. The village falls away behind you. By the top your breath is coming short, and the wind off the sea has teeth.

The churchyard is small and old, ringed by a dry-stone wall leaning every which way like drunk men holding each other up. The headstones inside all face the water. Just past the gate there's fresh-turned earth, a neat brown mouth with a spade standing in the spoil-heap.

Hollis sees you first. The grey lurcher unfolds himself from the foot of the gate and comes down the last few yards to meet you, tail low and slow. He presses his long skull into your hip without a sound. To the Sight he's a smudge of grey smoke with eyes, and the eyes are tired.

Brother Anselm Kade is sitting on the wall beside the gate with his hands loose between his knees. He looks as though he hasn't moved since moonrise. His eyes are red-rimmed. His mourning band is a strip of black cloth tied neat and tight, the way a soldier would tie it.

"Sister." He takes you in: the orange, the white braid, the empty hands. No sword, no staff. Something in his weathered face approves of that and doesn't say so.

"He's in the chapel." A tip of the head toward the little stone building behind him. "I washed him myself. Wrapped him." A pause. "He was a Brother of the House. Someone should."

He rubs his face with one hand.

"Your sexton dug at first light, and talked the whole time." Something tired that could almost be a smile. "So I already know about Bett Pellow's youngest. And a goblin, apparently. And that the shrine-keeper's well-woman has been seen *smiling*, which I gather is unprecedented."

Then the smile goes, and he looks at you straight.

"Will you speak for him at the bell?" It's quiet. "I'll stand there either way. But I'd rather it was you."

Hollis leans into your hands with a long, low sigh, the sound of a dog who has been on duty all night and has finally been told he's a good boy.

When you come against Kade's chest, he goes stiff as a fencepost. For a long moment he doesn't move at all. He smells of cold stone, lamp-smoke, and the faint clean sharpness of the washing-water. Then, slowly, as if he's had to remember how it's done, one big hand comes up and settles flat between your shoulder blades. It doesn't pat. It just stays there. A soldier's comfort, steady as a wall.

He says nothing while you cry. The wind does all the talking.

When you step back and point, he looks down at himself. There's a grey-black handprint of charcoal on his good dark coat, right over the heart, with a long smear trailing from it.

He stares at it.

Then something cracks in his weathered face, and out comes a short, startled laugh, rusty, as though it hasn't been used in a while. "*Well,*" he says. "That'll take some explaining to the Almoner." It shakes out of him again, quieter. "Gods. Look at the pair of us."

Hollis thumps his tail against the gatepost.

"Hold still." Kade digs in the scrip at his belt and comes out with a fold of plain black wool. "In my trade, you always carry black," he says, without any particular weight. He cuts a strip with a small knife and ties it around your left arm, neat and tight, a soldier's knot, just above the charcoal-smudged linen. He doesn't take the old one off.

"Keep that one under it," he says, tugging the knot square. "You made it with the boy."

He sits back down on the wall. Behind him, the chapel door is a dark slot in grey stone. Below, the sea glitters all the way out to the Teeth.

"Noon, then," he says.

The way down is easier than the way up, and the sea keeps you company the whole time, glittering on your left.

The cottage door scrapes. Inside it's dim and warm and smells of peat and fish-and-barley. Min is still a small grey knot on the hearthstone, sunk in the red dusk Asher is holding over him. Asher gives you a gold flicker of greeting and doesn't dare do more for fear of spilling his light.

Mira is at the table, sleeves pushed up, with the horehound laid out in front of her, studied and untouched. She takes one look at your face and gets up.

"No," she says, before you've even set the satchel down. "Soup. Then sleep." She's already ladling. "The horehound will keep two hours. You won't."

The brass mortar goes up on the high shelf, wrapped in your linen, safe beside the salt crock. The soup is hot, salty, and thick with barley, and you eat it all without stopping to talk. Somewhere in the second half of the bowl your eyelids start to win.

Mira steers you to the pallet by the fire. It still smells faintly of steam and small boy.

"I'll wake you," she says, pulling the quilt over you. "Before the bell. You have my word."

You don't hear her move away.

## Session 5 wrap - rulings and design notes (2026-10-01)
- **OK (Lee ruling) - Hook alterations are always FREE.** Player-driven, a separate channel from the one-improvement limit, meant as a relief valve. Supersedes the open item in CLAUDE.md that says Hook advancement uses the improvement slot. Reducing a Hook still needs testing.

Against the purely mundane, at best psychometry (the mood of past handlers). Good model of a Trick naming its mechanism (tricks.md).
- **@@ UNCOMMITTED - Spell endings: "the world tends to put things back."** Lee's principle: when a spell ends, the world generally restores what the spell changed. Stone Shape is the test case. A hearthstone shaped into a bowl reverts to a hearthstone's SHAPE when the spell ends, but stays WHERE it now is (no teleport).
  - GM corollaries @@*: (1) Matter that cannot resume its old shape where it now sits, such as a bridge drawn out of a cliff, CRUMBLES. This fits the canon flavor line "he let it crumble to dust." (2) Only the spell's change reverts. Mundane work done on the shaped stone in the meantime stays. (3) Permanence is bought, not free: Persistent holds it while there is no reason it shouldn't, and Enchantment (Karma) or Artifice makes it stay. This gives Artifice a clear job. (4) Possible spirit route: if the place's own genius ACCEPTS the new shape (Accords; a Conjuror's negotiation), the world may not pull it back. Proposed, not ruled.
  - Consistency check against existing effects: Fax Iacta's light simply ends; Tanglebones/Entangle roots spring back to where they were. Same principle.
EOF
cp gap-log.md "out/2026-09-30 PLAYTEST - S04 Gap Log - Caria.md" 2>>stderr.log; echo ok</parameter>
<parameter name="description">Log the spell-ending principle and wrap rulings in the gap log</parameter>
</tool>
```
Yes. It feels right, and it's *consistent*, which matters more. Fax Iacta's light simply stops. Tanglebones' roots spring back to where they grew. A shaped stone going back to its shape, wherever it happens to be sitting, is the same principle. The world remembers *form*. It doesn't remember *address*.

That one rule produces some nice consequences, which I've logged as *@@** for you to accept or strike:

1. **What can't go home falls apart.** Draw a bridge out of a cliff face and release it, and that stone can't become cliff again from midair. So it crumbles. That's your canon flavor line, *"he let it crumble to dust,"* explained by the rule rather than by decoration. That feels like a sign we've got it right.
2. **Only the spell's change reverts.** If Mira scratches her initials into the bowl while it's a bowl, the initials stay, on a hearthstone, as a weird little fossil of the spell. That's a good detail for the curious player.
3. **Permanence is bought, not free.** A Persistent shape holds until there's a reason it shouldn't. Enchantment (Karma) or Artifice makes it *stay*. That gives Artifice a crisp job description at last: *the craft of making the world forget to put things back.*
4. **The spirit route, which is a proposal only:** if the genius of a place *accepts* the new shape, by Accords negotiation, a Conjuror's errand, maybe the world doesn't tug it back. That's Spellweaving and Conjuring braided together, and very much her.

All of that is in the gap log now.

So is it Stone Shape for the fourth known spell? Once you nod, I'll build the S05 package, one file at a time: summary first, then the sheet, the gap log, and the ledger.

<body>

<h1>Session 5 - Tears Are Water</h1>
<p class="sub">Level One solo playtest, Averond - Caria Greenhaven, Initiate of the Monastery of Strife. GM: Lilita. Played 2026-09-30/10-01. Counted as two sessions for advancement (split at sleep, Mira's hearth).</p>

<details open><summary>At a glance</summary>
<p>A day and a night on the coast. Caria meets Mira Thousand-Voices with open hands and learns that the thing Mira burned on the beach had been a girl - a small one - which puts a name from the Monastery kitchens in her mouth and fear in her heart. She swears an oath to a starveling goblin, sits up all night with a fisherwife's croupy son, pays an undine with the one secret she is most ashamed of, and helps an old forge-fire touch the sea.</p>
<p>By morning, Saltwind is starting to talk about the Monastery girl who wouldn't take a copper.</p>
<p>Ends at Mira's hearth as the noon bell begins to toll for Brother Aubric.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 1 - The Basin and the Wall</summary>
<p>At Susheil's basin Caria finds herself crying again, and laughing, hands raised to the sea: tears are water too. Thousand-Voices arrives with Nell, an undine riding in her waterskin. Caria shows Shimmer open, empty hands - the message from the first night, when Shimmer expected oil and a torch - and the water grudges her a truce.</p>
<p>She prostrates herself to Mira as she did to Karinna and offers restitution for her Order's wayward hands. She can't say Aubric's name. Mira sits down on the cobbles to be level with her and doesn't let go of her hand.</p>
<blockquote>"Aubric was my friend. How can I help?"</blockquote>
<p>Mira offers her hearth. Caria accepts guest-right, and her friends in the fire-pot are made welcome: "a hearth is for fires."</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 2 - Mira's Hearth</summary>
<p>A turf-roofed cottage tucked into the cliff west of the village. Caria falls asleep on the hearthstone mid-sentence. Asher goes down the anchor line to give the Weeping Court her love, and the House sends back a warm leaf.</p>
<p>At dusk, Ivro's letter is delivered into the right hand; its watching spark winks out, content. Over fish-and-barley stew Mira tells what Calder said he was hunting - the Almoner's "property," a sick servant, "it" one breath and "him" the next - and Caria tells her what walked: Hospitaller Aubric, on a leash, toward Mira's door.</p>
<p>Then Mira says it was two. The one they burned on the beach, with e'Di and Shimmer and every drop of lamp oil in Saltwind, had been small. A girl, once. Caria hears the kitchen maids whispering that no one has seen the girl in weeks, and sorts what she knows from what she has heard and what she fears: Wenna Tarro, twelve, surety for her father's grain, in the west wing.</p>
<blockquote>"I trust Kade with my life and my loved ones - if I have any left."</blockquote>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 3 - Min</summary>
<p>Mira's household has another member: Min, a starveling juvenile goblin, one-eared, cataract-eyed and club-footed, who keeps her fire under a formal Accord. He smells Hobbe-fire on the guest. Caria kneels to his height and asks what she owes him. His terms: never tell any Hobbe where he is, and the sneaky-spark keeps his fire by day. Asher is thrilled.</p>
<p>Caria makes it larger: Min is her sacred trust, and she will defend the household that named her guest even if he no longer lives there. Min is horrified to be over-paid and offers his whole catch. She accepts one mussel, shared - steamed open by Asher on his new fire - and thanks him in the sky-tongue. He answers, flawlessly, before he can stop himself: <em>Received and witnessed. So it is bound.</em></p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 4 - Holes Tied Together With String</summary>
<p>Mira teaches her to mend nets. Caria gives Mira herbs, and Mags's honey, carried from the Monastery kitchens "for the shrine-keeper." Old Bellows, through Min, admits peat is cow-fire and asks for applewood - and when is the sea? Mira knows: a smith's fire knows the quench. Dawn, at the cove, when the sea breathes out.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 5 - The Croup</summary>
<p>Past midnight, Bett Pellow comes up the cliff path with her youngest, Daw, whooping and dusky-lipped. She came for Thousand-Voices and finds the Monastery woman instead. Caria's Sight finds the swelling and the fright feeding it; she treats both, counting breaths in a cheerful voice and talking to the mother strictly in the relieved past tense. It works.</p>
<p>Then the lesson: never ask a priest of Strife for help - bring the problem, as Bett did. Fire is a teacher. And: if you want to save your boy, you keep calm. In the black hour the croup comes back, and Bett is already counting before Caria is awake.</p>
<blockquote>"You're not that." - Bett, of the man whose cudgel broke her Jory's collarbone.</blockquote>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 6 - The Quench</summary>
<p>At the cove at dawn Shimmer names her price for letting a fire into her water: a secret Caria has told no one. Caria gives her the true one, and weeps. The undine takes her tears too, and keeps them. "Water is the one thing it cannot burn."</p>
<p>Old Bellows meets the sea through Mira's borrowed voice - "Six hundred years I've been quenching nails in a bucket!" - and comes up tempered: black as jet, his heart a live ember sealed inside. He asks to be carried home to his forge someday, with a story no fire in Averond can match.</p>
<p>Climbing back, Caria tells Mira about Jem and the lonely House that wants a tenant who won't fade. Mira sees the shape of it, and every reason for caution. "But..."</p>
</details>

<details><summary>Scene 7 - Morning in Saltwind</summary>
<p>Bett's back door is open to her, "and that's not a payment." The net-woman tests her knots: "They'll hold." At the well-house Caria borrows Karinna's grandmother's brass mortar, reads the pain in the old keeper's hands with the Sight, and teaches Nell the brine, the willow, the oil - and a different story every night. Karinna closes her fist, all the way, three times.</p>
<p>At the churchyard gate Brother Kade has kept vigil all night and washed the Hospitaller himself. She weeps into his coat; he ties her a proper black band over the charcoal one. "Keep that one under it. You made it with the boy." Soup, sleep, and the bell.</p>
</details>

<details><summary>People met</summary>
<table>
<tr><th>Who</th><th>What Caria knows</th></tr>
<tr><td>Mira Thousand-Voices</td><td>Itinerant keeper of the coast's neglected shrines; Conjuror; host. Aubric set her arm when she was nine. Burned the first ghola.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Shimmer</td><td>Mira's undine. A truce, a secret kept, tears taken.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Min</td><td>"Little Target." Mira's goblin, keeper of her fire. Bound to Caria by oath and one shared mussel.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Bett, Daw and Jory Pellow</td><td>Fisher family. Daw's croup; Jory's collarbone and grudge. Their back door is open.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Karinna and Nell</td><td>Susheil's keeper and her guide. Old hands, a brass mortar, a story every night.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Brother Kade and Hollis</td><td>Keeping vigil at the churchyard. Burial at noon.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Old Tobin</td><td>Saltwind's sexton, no relation to Ivro's clerk. Talks.</td></tr>
</table>
</details>

<p>Full detail, including New-GM notes on knowledge drift and compaction drift, is in the gap log.</p>
</details>

One broader Maneuver at depth beats two narrow ones at 1, and it suits the streamline principle. Worth a line in maneuvers.md: you may fold a new rank into an existing Maneuver and broaden its name, with GM consent.

Resolution: she accepted a token payment (one mussel, shared), which concluded the exchange, and Min filed a contingent clause: "debt when you DO, not before." A clean example of the Accords pushing toward balance; worth including in conjuring.md's Accords section.
- **Hooks as currency - an NPC spirit's Hook sets its price.** Shimmer's Hook "A Keeper of Secrets" made her price a secret. The player chose the most costly true one. Paying with secrets works beautifully as an Accords payment, and it naturally produces character revelation. Good GM advice: let a spirit's Hook name its price.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# L1 Simple Pool roller. Usage: roll.sh EL [extra_effort_dice] [label]
EL=${1:?EL required}; XE=${2:-0}; LABEL=${3:-roll}
N=$((EL+XE)); T=0; D=""
for ((i=0;i<N;i++)); do r=$((RANDOM%2)); D+="$r "; T=$((T+r)); done
echo "[$LABEL] EL$EL +${XE}XE -> ${N}d[0-1]: $D= $T"
if (( T > EL )); then echo "  OVER EL -> total failure (effect 0)"
elif (( T == 0 && N >= 3 )); then echo "  ALL ZEROES -> EXTREME FAILURE"
elif (( T == 0 )); then echo "  zero -> failure"
elif (( T == EL && T == N && N >= 3 )); then echo "  ALL MAX & = EL -> EXTREME SUCCESS"
else echo "  result $T"; fi
```
  Run as `./roll.sh EL 0 "label" 2>>stderr.log`. NEVER `2>/dev/null`.

On Boost caps - you're right, nothing in the rules caps them. 
I totally get why you bring it up. I'd *like* to avoid adding more rules, so if it works as it is, which it kind of does, I want any rule we add to Canon to earn its keep. 

The current logic is that a genuine skill in something tangentially relevant can *carry* a lesser skill in whatever you're actually doing. Being really good at Second Sight gives her a clear path of action, and while what *actually* rescued Daw was Healer, and maybe Performer, with totally appropriate Synergy in that particular case...being able to *see* exactly what the problem was, and where, gave her real confidence she could show Bett without that hesitation a mother detects and latches onto.

EL is *slippery* though, and if you start zooming in past that you get Role + Maneuvers, and it devolves into too much fiddly math. Even as an option, a *general* option needs to be as simple and consistent as possible, something a GM might have just improvised on their own, *which is really the point*. The options are basically just teaching the game runners the ropes, where the levers and dials fit well without derailing the system, so that in the middle of a game they *can* just improvise something that "feels about right" and keep the game moving...which is something we really need to say in the book. :)

I checked before agreeing, and **assist-rule.md already caps one kind of Boost**: help from gear with its own capabilities is limited to *your* rank in the relevant Role. The Demon Bow gives a Sniper 1 archer exactly 1 point, *"because you aren't skilled enough to leverage what it offers."*

So the book already has one cap, and it's narrower and much stricter than yours. That matters if your option goes in. A reader who sees both will assume they contradict each other unless the book says why they differ. The distinction is a good one, and it matches your reasoning:

- **Outside help** (a bow, a ship, a familiar's gift) is limited by your skill to *use* it.
- **Your own knowledge** isn't limited that way. Real skill in a neighboring field can *carry* a weaker one. The Sight didn't heal Daw, but it gave Caria the certainty a frightened mother can read in a healer's hands.

Your option, *"a Boost adds no more dice than the EL it's boosting,"* is just what a GM might improvise mid-game, so it's the right kind of option. And the S5 case sits exactly on the line: Boost 5 on Healer EL5. It passes, with nothing to spare. That's as tidy a test as you could ask for.

In the gap log I've changed the old @@ OPEN entry to @@ UNCOMMITTED, as an *optional guideline, not a rule*, with the assist-rule precedent noted beside it. Your larger point has its own @@ MISSING entry: *options exist to teach GMs where the levers are, so they can improvise "about right" and keep play moving.* I'd argue that line belongs near the front of the GM section, because a lot of the rest of the book only makes sense in its light.

**Session 6 - The Words**

You wash your face in the cold rain-barrel water. Shimmer stays politely still. You braid your hair tight with the silver pin. The black band on your arm sits over the grey one. Min is a small knot asleep in Asher's red dusk, and he doesn't stir as you go out.

The bell tolls the whole way up the hill.

You aren't alone on the lane. That's the first thing. Doors open as you pass, and people come out in their good shawls and patched coats and fall in behind you and Mira without a word.

At the churchyard gate you stop.

There are perhaps forty of them, more than Saltwind can easily spare at noon on a fishing day. Karinna is there on Nell's arm, having made the hill at her own slow pace. Old Mirna stands with her son's wife, the one who tested your knots. Harl Pennock and young Davey have their caps in their hands. Fennick hovers at the very back, turning his hat round and round.

The Pellows stand together: Bett with Daw on her hip, and a broad man with two fingers missing from his right hand who must be Hal. Beside them is a tall, hollow-cheeked boy with his arm strapped across his chest in a sling. Jory. His eyes find the orange robe and stay on it, flat and hard.

And by the wall, in her oilskin, with her grey braid over her shoulder, is Dasha Korrin. Jem stands beside her. He's still too thin, but he's upright, the charcoal band on his arm the twin of yours. He sees you and his face does something complicated.

Inside the gate, the brown grave is open. The long white bundle lies on a plank bier beside it, washed and wrapped by a soldier's careful hands. Old Tobin leans on his spade. Hollis lies at the foot of the bier with his head on his paws.

Brother Kade stands at the head of the grave. He looks across the crowd at you and gives you one small nod.

The bell stops.

In the silence, all you can hear is the sea.

The cobbles are cold. Doors open as you pass. People in their good shawls see the Monastery girl walking barefoot in ash and fall silent and step in behind you. By the time you reach the hill there's a long, quiet tail of them following up the lane.

At the gate there are forty souls, perhaps more.

Karinna is there on Nell's arm. Old Mirna stands with her daughter-in-law. Harl Pennock and Davey have their caps in their fists, and Fennick is at the back, turning his hat round and round. The Pellows are together: Bett with Daw, broad Hal with his two-fingered hand, and Jory, tall and hollow-cheeked, his arm strapped across his chest. His eyes find you, ready to hate the orange, and *falter* at the ash and the bare feet. For a heartbeat something uncertain crosses his face. Then his jaw sets again.

By the wall stand Dasha Korrin in her oilskin and Jem beside her, the charcoal band on his arm the twin of yours.

Inside, the grave is open. The long white bundle lies on its plank. Old Tobin leans on his spade. Hollis has his head on his paws at the foot of the bier.

Kade, at the head of the grave, looks at your bare feet, and then at your face, and nods once.

Mira's arms close around you without a word. She smells of peat and salt, and she holds you the way you held Daw: steady and unhurried, as if she has all the time in the world.

For a long moment nobody moves.

Then there's the tap of a stick on cold ground.

**Karinna** doesn't step forward. She only lifts her face toward the bier. "Thirty-one springs," she says, in a voice like old rope. "Every spring, on his circuit, for thirty-one years. And never once came to my well-house without a little jar of something for these hands." She holds them up, oiled and knotted, and closes them slowly into fists. "He'd be glad of who came after him."

**Hal Pellow** clears his throat twice before anything will come out. "Took two of these." He holds up the ruined hand. "Sat up with me three nights. Never asked a copper. Only said to feed the hungry." His voice goes rough. "We still do. We still *do*."

**Mira** speaks into your hair, low, but they all hear her. "I fell off the harbor wall when I was nine. He set my arm on the stones and said, 'You'll mend.'" A breath. "I did." Then her voice changes for a single line, warmer, drier, and somehow older: "*Go on, then. Eat something.*" Half the crowd laughs through their tears, because every one of them has heard him say it.

Last is **Brother Kade**. He stands at the head of the grave with his hand on the dog's head and speaks soldier-plain, without any grace in it at all.

"I didn't know him living. I carried him two days." His jaw works. "He was a Brother of my House. He was murdered, and then he was *used*." His eyes go, very deliberately, to the back of the crowd, to the Almoner's clerk with his crushed hat. "I'll say so to anyone who asks. And I'll write it."

Fennick doesn't reach for his notebook.

Nobody else speaks. The wind sighs in the long grass.

Old Tobin and Kade each take up a rope, and they look to you.

The first notes come out thin and cracked. By the third they've found the floor of your chest, and after that they don't break again.

It's the old one, the dirge every novice learns: *the fire returns to the fire, the breath to the wind, the water to the sea.* Plain words in the sky-tongue, set to a melody that goes down and down like steps into cool earth.

And they *know* it.

You see it hit them on the second line. Old Mirna's head comes up. Karinna's lips part. One cracked voice at the back starts humming under you, then another, then a scatter of them. They don't have the Celestial, only the tune, because a circuit healer sang this same dirge over their husbands and their mothers and their drowned sons for thirty years. They're singing him home with his own song.

Hollis lifts his long grey muzzle and keens on the long notes, soft and true, like wind in a chimney.

For anyone with the Sight, the churchyard grass begins to glow. Small lights rise out of it, scores of them, faint as sparks drifting from a hearth: the little spirits of an old burying-ground, taking up a prayer in the language they were made to carry and bearing it upward. Mira's breath catches against your hair. At the head of the grave Kade's eyes have gone wide, fixed on the air above the bier.

Even the gulls have gone quiet.

On the last verse, *the water to the sea*, the ropes creak. Kade and Old Tobin lower him, hand over hand, slow and even, into the brown earth. The sailcloth settles. The rosemary is still on his breast.

The last note goes out over the water and doesn't come back.

Old Tobin wipes his face on his sleeve. Then he bends, scoops up a handful of the cold spoil, and holds it out to you in his cracked palm, the way it's done here. The speaker throws first.

The earth is cold and wet and heavier than it ought to be.

You don't throw it. You hold it out over the dark mouth of the grave and squeeze until it hurts. A sound leaves you that isn't a word. Then you let your fingers open, and it falls in crumbs onto the pale sailcloth and the green sprig.

Your hand is empty. You draw it slowly down one cheek, then the other: earth over ash over tears.

Then you turn and walk away from all of them, down the hill toward the sea.

Nobody stops you.

The grass is cold and wet under your bare feet. Below, the harbor wall and the grey shingle are bright with spray, and the surf is coming in long and low. Water. *Tears are water.* You mean to sit down in it. You mean to put your feet in the cold salt and let it have whatever it wants...

The churchyard wall goes past your shoulder. Then the ground isn't where it should be, and the sky turns over slowly like a page.

---

Something warm and bony thumps against your side. Hollis is whining, his long nose shoving at your face.

Then come boots, and a voice you know. *"I've got her."* Kade, again. Arms under your knees and shoulders, and you're lifted the way he lifted you out of the reeds at the Ford. His coat smells of cold stone and lamp-smoke and the charcoal handprint you left on it.

Mira's voice somewhere close: *"The shingle first. She wants the sea. Then home."*

Behind them, quick footsteps. Jem, maybe. Another, heavier and uneven, could be Jory.

The surf is louder.

Then everything goes soft and grey and far away, and for a while there's nothing at all.

**The Shingle**

Cold comes first. It's at your feet: a slow, rhythmic cold, going and coming back. Then sound: pebbles rolling over each other, hissing, settling.

You're lying on something hard and uneven, with your head on something soft. Something heavy and waxed and smelling of tar is wrapped around you. An oilskin. *Korrin's.*

You open your eyes.

The sky is white and high. Mira's face hangs upside-down above you, salt-stiff hair blowing, and her hand is resting on your brow as if she's been keeping it there for a long while.

"There you are," she says.

You're on the harbor shingle below the churchyard. Your bare feet are down at the lip of the surf, and the sea is washing over them, cold and patient, carrying the ash and the grave-earth away in thin grey threads. You meant to sit in it. Somebody made sure you did.

Kade's expression doesn't change by so much as a hair. He watches the hound work the boot over with the gravity of a man reviewing a report.

"Then the vapors are going around, Sister," he says. "I'd heard it was a hard season for them."

Hollis gets the last of the broth out of the heel, sneezes once (onion, or leather, or indignity) and sits back on his haunches. He looks up at Caria with the calm, total loyalty of a creature that has just decided where it's sleeping tonight.

Kade notices it too. "He doesn't sleep in *my* space," he says mildly. "He sleeps wherever the warmest feet are." A small tilt of the head toward her soup-soaked boot. "And tonight that's the Sister who fed him half a bowl through her stocking. I'll sleep very well, thank you."

Hollis thumps his tail against the floorboards twice, as if signing the agreement.

Down the hall, Hal's round has come apart into several rounds at once. Two of Korrin's drovers were close enough to catch the end of Kade's verse, and they grin into their cups with the special joy of men who never expected to hear *that* in the same room as a robe. At the fire Jory heard none of the words, only her laugh. He looks over, and something in his shoulders lets go.

The light through the shutters has gone the color of weak tea. On the bench Fennick has lifted his face out of his hands. Mira is still talking low and steady, and Karinna is still very carefully not listening.

Your boot squelches when you shift your weight.

*(Lilita, perched on the rim of the ale jug and fanning herself with a scrap of smoke: "Vapors. Truly. I've seen you dissect a goat, darling.")*

The light goes. Mirna works her way down the hall with a taper, lamp by lamp, grumbling at each wick as if it had personally wronged her. The drovers' songs settle into a low murmur. Kade stays beside you without being asked; Hollis settles across your soggy boot like a warm, damp sandbag.

On the bench Mira talks for a long time. She keeps her voice level. Her hands mostly stay in her lap, except once, when she shapes something about the height of a child in the air between them and then lets it drop. Fennick doesn't interrupt. Twice he starts to speak and stops. Karinna sits on Mira's other side with Nell asleep against her, and goes on not listening with tremendous skill.

At last Fennick nods, once, the way a man signs for a delivery he didn't want. He goes back to the bench where you sat together, finds his hat, and turns it around in his hands. Then he crosses the hall to you.

He's steadier than you expected. His face is grey, but his voice is a clerk's voice, plain and in order.

"The Corvane line," he says. "I audit the house books at the turn of each month. Seven weeks ago that line read *closed*. I initialed it, Sister." He touches the hat brim with one ink-stained finger, right where a mark would sit. "I put my mark beside it. I thought, *good, someone's paid their debt*. I thought it was a *tidy* line."

He breathes once, carefully.

"I don't know her name. Your Keeper doesn't either. Sureties are entered under the debtor, so the books say *Corvane* and nothing else. The father's name is in my head and the child's isn't anywhere." He looks at you directly for the first time since the soup. "Is there something your Order does? For someone with no name, and nothing left to bury?"

Across the hall Mira meets your eyes over Karinna's head and gives you one small nod. *He heard all of it. He's still standing.*

You don't need to say it aloud. You just think his name the way you'd tug a familiar thread, and up on the bluff, at Mira's hearth, something small and bright looks up.

*Asher. Would you like to show off a little?*

His answer comes back before you've finished the thought, warm as a cat landing in your lap. *YES. Lamps? Lamps in a hall, with people watching? Yes yes yes-*

Then a pause. You feel him stop dead, the way a child stops halfway through grabbing a sweet.

*...She said hearth.*

Shimmer. Two days ago at Mira's door: *the little one keeps to the hearth and stops asking what burns.* He was doused once already, the first time he came sneaking along this coast, and he remembers it in his wick.

He takes the problem apart the way a small clever creature does, mostly hopefully. *Mirna's pit is a hearth. A real one, a big one. If I go to the pit and throw sparks up to the wicks, the sparks are mine, but I'm still in the hearth. Is that keeping to it?* A worried flicker. *Did she mean* Mira's *hearth? Or* a *hearth? She didn't say.*

Then, very earnestly: *You decide. You're the one who talks to her keeper.*

In the kitchen behind you, Mira hasn't turned around. Her hands have stopped moving among the cups, though. With the Third Eye she saw your attention go out along that thread like a line paid out to sea, and she knows exactly who's just been asked to play.

Mirna is still squinting up at you with the taper held to her chest.

Up on the bluff, Asher takes *it doesn't hurt to ask* exactly as literally as only a very small, very brave fire can.

You feel him do it. He pulls himself up tall on Mira's hearth, tall for a spark anyway, and turns to face the rain-barrel by the door, the one that put him out once. Then he *asks*. He gives her your words, in order: Mirna's hearths, her candles, her sconces, her lamps. The right things burn. Nothing else.

The barrel is quiet a long moment. Then its surface lifts, one slow ripple, and an answer comes back through Asher to you. It's cool and wet and amused:

*For that house's fires. When the widow asks. Not the girl. Not the spark.*

Then the water is just water again.

Asher is very nearly incandescent. *She said YES. I asked her MYSELF and she didn't put me OUT.* A beat, and then, scrupulously: *...when the widow asks. I'll wait. I'm waiting. I'm very good at waiting.* (He isn't.)

In the kitchen behind you, a gust off the water rattles the yard door in its frame, and a fine salt spray hisses through the cracks across the flagstones. Mira looks up from the cups at the door and smiles at it as you'd smile at an old friend who's walked in without knocking.

You open both eyes.

Mirna hasn't moved. At *permission from the sea* her mouth went thin as a seam. She stands there with the taper and looks at you for a long moment, at a girl from the mountain with her eyes shut, asking the water for something. Whatever passes through the old woman's face, she puts it away before you can read it.

"Ask her, then," Mirna says at last, gruffly. "She owes this house."

She doesn't explain. She just waits, taper held to her chest, under the three dark lamps.

Mirna holds your look a moment longer. Then she turns, not to you but to the seaward wall, where the shutters are rattling softly with the evening wind off the water.

"You heard her," she says to it, in exactly the voice she'd use to haggle over a basket of herring. "Lamps lit. Fish left be. Nobody's roof afire. That's my asking."

She doesn't move. Then, lower, so that only you're close enough to hear:

"You've had enough of mine. You can give me this."

You don't know what it means. But you know the sound of a debt being called in.

Up on the bluff, something lets go like a loosed arrow.

Asher comes down the cliff path as a streak of gold, too fast to follow, and drops in through the smoke-hole into the fire-pit with a *whumph* that sends the drovers' heads up. For one heartbeat the whole pit blazes blue at the roots and gold at the heart. Then he pulls himself in, banks the fire down to a low, even, steady glow, and flicks three sparks straight up to the crossbeam, one, two, three.

The three dark lamps bloom alight. They're small and clean and steady.

Mira shakes her head at the apology. "You didn't rope me, Sister. I was there first."

She turns her cup a quarter-turn on the scrubbed boards and looks into it while she answers, as if the beer were the beach.

"Lamp oil on open sand doesn't make a pyre. It burns hot and fast and then it's gone, and the wind takes half of it. We burned it till there was nothing left that could move." A small pause. "There were bones. Small ones. Black."

Fennick makes a sound in his throat and says nothing.

"I couldn't put her in Tobin's yard. The taint was in them, and the priest would have dug her up looking for his property." She says *property* the way you'd hold something dead by the tail. "So I took them up the far end of the beach, above the tideline, and laid a ring of salt, and asked Shimmer's leave, and built a cairn over them. Small. You'd walk past it." Her mouth twists. "I go there sometimes."

Then she reaches into her shawl, slowly, as though her hand isn't sure it means to. She brings out a twist of faded cloth and sets it on the table beside the lamp, and unfolds it with two fingers.

There's a little heap of dress-hooks, warped by the heat. And one button: cast brass, the size of a thumbnail, blackened on one side. Something is stamped into its face, a mark too small and too scorched to make out from where you sit.

"The metal didn't burn," Mira says. "I kept the button to pray on. Every prayer has weight." She looks up, at you and then at the clerk. "I've not shown it to anyone."

Kade has gone very still on his stool by the door. He was sent across half of Averond to fetch what lies on that cloth. Under the table, Hollis lifts his head and whines once, very low, at something none of the living can smell.

Fennick is staring at the button the way a man stares at a sum he already knows the answer to.

The words come out of you in the sky-tongue. It's the clean, terrible language of contracts, and your mouth knows it better than it should. *Open, you son of a bitch. You* show *me.*

The breath behind them comes out *yellow*. Sulphur hazes over the lamp and curls under the drying fish, and every soul in that kitchen smells it. Fennick's head snaps up; he's smelled it on you before. Hollis surges to his feet with every hair standing, but he presses *against* you, not away. Like calls to like. The splinter *opens*.

Your brimstone has looked at that small, starving, broken-off thing and wants to *eat it*. Kin calls to kin, and the bigger fire wants the smaller. Your hands are shaking because some part of you is hungry.

**Then the thread.** You follow it north with the Eye, a hair-thin bruise through the dark, up the coast and inland and *down*, under stone. At the end of it something vast is lying in the dark. It's chained and patient and mostly asleep. The splinter was broken off *that*.

And right beside the chain the thread runs through a taste you know: rancid incense, wounded pride. You burned it out of a leash in the sand at Tanner's Ford.

*Calder.* His hand is on that chain.

As you look, the vast thing **stirs**. Only a little. It shifts in its sleep the way a dog shifts when it dreams. It doesn't wake, and it doesn't look. You feel the shiver of its turning come back down the thread to you like a tremor through a rope.

You close the Eye. Or it closes. You aren't sure which.

The sulphur is still hanging over the lamp.

Mira flexes her fingers in yours and considers them with professional interest.

"You've a grip like a net-winch," she says. "I'll live." The corner of her mouth twitches. "Bett will be jealous. She only got her son's croup out of you."

Then the twitch fades. She looks at you a moment longer than the joke needs. With the Eye she saw the yellow flare go up off you like a struck match, and under it she saw something else, something in you leaning toward that brass. She doesn't name it. You watch her decide not to, and fold it away somewhere careful, the way she folded the cloth.

"You went a long way north just then," is all she says. She doesn't ask what you found. She'll wait until you're ready to tell it.

She gets to her feet, knees cracking on the flagstones, and lifts the latch on the yard door. Cold sea air rolls in at once, wet and clean and salt-heavy. It takes the sulphur haze off the lamp and carries it out over the shingle, and the surf swallows it. The drying fish sway on their cords. For a breath the whole kitchen smells only of the sea.

By the hall door Kade takes his hand off his knife, finger by finger, as if he's had to remind it.

Fennick lets out a breath he seems to have been holding since the Celestial. Without a word he reaches across and slides your cup of small beer back in front of you. His hand isn't quite steady. It's the most practical thing anyone in the room can think to do, and he does it.

Hollis lies back down across your feet with a long, aggrieved sigh.

The cloth sits folded on the table. Under it the brass is awake, and you know it. But it's just a button, and you're just a girl with a cup of beer and three people waiting.

Hollis receives the pat and the slander with equal dignity. He thumps his tail once against the flagstones, as if to say he'd heard worse.

"He'll take the blame," Kade says from the door. "He's taken worse for me."

Then you lay it out, glass sliver and gangrene and the great dark lode under the Mountain. Kade listens the way he listened to Hal's goat story at the meal, all the way to the end, without moving. When you say *somehow has a leash on it*, something professional surfaces in his face. You've watched it happen before: the finder taking hold of a problem.

"Not a leash," he says. "Not on a thing that size. You don't hold something like that with rope and spite." He nods down at the dog across your feet. "Hollis is bound to me. I know what it took. Binding takes a *name*, Sister. Its True Name." He lets that sit. "So either Calder has the name of whatever's under that mountain..." A small pause. "Or somebody gave it to him."

Fennick has been staring at the folded cloth. He speaks without looking up, very quietly, the way a man speaks when he's adding a column he doesn't like the sum of.

"And *somehow* is usually *paid for*." He turns his cup slowly between his ink-stained fingers. "The sureties are entered in the Almoner's books. The Almoner's office draws the per diem. The Almoner's office pays the cooks who carry the bread to the west wing." He swallows. "I enter those lines. In a fair hand."

Kade's eyes go flat as slate. The Almoner is who he reports to. He doesn't say anything at all.

Mira has drifted back to stand in the open yard door with her shawl pulled tight. She's looking out past the shingle at the dark end of the beach, where the tideline curves away under the stars. She hasn't said a word since she opened the latch.

The sea breathes in and out. Your thumb keeps circling the rim of your cup.
